item.title: Is there a way to SUGGEST new classes?
item.content:encoded:
Is there a way to suggest a theoretical esoteric class despite the lack of an article? If not, would someone be willing to try writing for a new esoteric?

If you're wondering what my idea is, let's propose the following thought experiment:

+ show block
– hide block

A researcher is investigating some theoretical elements of the periodic table, when suddenly, they create samples of the entire eighth row of the table non-anomalously, but the elements themselves have anomalous properties. The Foundation gets word of it, does Their Thing TM, and writes some new article for these elements. It's Safe… except a few days later, someone else makes the same elements. So, to react to the fact that the anomalous elements can be made non-anomalously, a new esoteric is created:

Aedificunt
(Latin for "they build")
Anomaly can be created by non-anomalous means, but is still anomalous in its own right.

Thank you!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
A lot of non-narritivistic classes actually make a lot of sense, like Archon and Kušum and Maksur. At least, it’s make sense that the Foundation would encounter anomalies that need to be left alone/uncontained/apart. In my opinion, though, a lot of other "established classes" violate the idea of an object class. Neither Eparch nor Gödel are connected to containment difficulty and function more as explanations of mechanics.

Even my own Ignosi violates the idea of an object class; "Item's discovery, even by the Foundation, must be prevented." begs the question of how hard prevention of discovery is. The reason I classify DRO-0001 (who is named Apollyon, to add to the confusion) as Ignosi instead of Keter is to signal that something is very different here. The Foundation sees this anomaly as such a threat they've created an object class to distinguish it.

I plan on tackling object classes in a future 001 proposal I'm writing about the Veil Incarnate. How do you classify the Veil, if it's an entity that can perpetuate its own existence? It's definitionally Thaumiel, but the Foundation isn't using it, strictly. Maybe Archon? What about Safe, if it's self-containing? And Keter if they do try to contain it — how the hell do you contain the Veil?

Such a silly idea, The Object Class — as though all of that one's children could be parsed into Safe, Euclid, and Keter. You couldn't do it, could you? You created a cacophony of esoterics to describe a cacophonous phenomenon: the anomalous.

I don't really know if we should be sticking to a stricter class system or if authors should be encouraged to do what they want, but people are still using esoterics, and more importantly, readers are confused by said esoterics. Hence the guide.

To actually answer your suggestion, I'll totally plug the Threat Levels. If I had an article where it made sense in the narrative to use a Threat Level, I would have.

Thanks for reading! Sorry for taking up your time.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If we really want to cut the frills, there's no reason to stop at SEKTEN.

+ show block
– hide block

We don't really need Keter, since the difference between that and Euclid is not qualitative but related to the complexity (and, depending who you ask, urgency) of containment procedures that the Safe/Euclid distinction already covers. We don't need Thaumiel because it boils down to a specific category of Euclid instruction. We don't even really need Explained; we can fold that right into Neutralized, since anything that becomes the former also effectively becomes the latter (especially as far as the SCP documentation is concerned). Distilled to their essence, the categories come down to "does not require interaction," "does require interaction," and "no longer anomalous."

Note that this is just a thought experiment; I have nothing against one-off classes and really like some of them (my favorite on this page is "infohazardous predator", which suggests an entirely more straightforward and comprehensive classification system altogether).

When I started reading the site, there were two things that struck me about the containment classes being these obscure words:
1) the Foundation must deal with all kinds of scary stuff on a large scale if they have the perspective to file it all in categories like this, which establishes their power and credibility right off the bat and
2) the choice to use these exotic, occult-sounding words instead of plain language suggests secrecy, hidden motives and methods, and the sense that even as someone with access to these in-universe files I'm not privy to what's really going on. This immediately creates a sense of tension by establishing the SCPF as an entity the reader can't trust.

That's a hell of a lot to convey in just three words, which is probably why the SEK system is so iconic. But seeing new categories pop up doesn't diminish either of those things I like about the system1, and innovation is pretty important if we want to wring another 10 years of content out of this premise.

tl;dr: in favor of oddball classes when they're cool and make articles better.

Footnotes
1. Except when it does, which happens occasionally

item.content:encoded:
I don't think a number of these entries should be on here. Just because an esoteric class is unique in usage doesn't make it feel like it has to be listed, unless it's one that needs explanation. For example, Keter/Friend is literally just Keter; why list that? Shaggy's Proposal is on that list twice due to its article fuckery, when its Apollyon usage can probably preclude it from being listed repeatedly. I'd rather see actual unique esoteric classes that could pass as being reusable rather than going by the ethos of literally listing every individual one. For example, Infohazardous Predator and Yesod, not At home and ??. Removing those, as well as removing redundant entries listed, would make the page feel tighter and more useful to someone who needs this.

I'll also criticize the inclusion of Joke Esoteric Classes here; a number of them feel disparate when taken outside of the context of their joke, and just feels like taking up page space, and even the ones that are "arguably" viable for standard documentation aren't because they're only used in a joke. Joke SCPs are the prime example of messing with object classes to achieve humor; listing them here feels humorless and seems to serve less purpose than the rest of the article does. The section could be excised with hardly anything missing.

Otherwise, the page looks good and is formatted nicely, and serves as a good resource for anyone who'd need this.

The Established table was created to help authors trying to find an esoteric class that might apply to their SCP. It is unlikely any new article will fit the definitions of Yesod and Netzach, and UNDEFINED is more the result of the anti-memetic qualities of the SCP it appears in. However, an author could write an SCP that is a direct threat to the O5s, broken into pieces, used to create SCPs, pending classification, debated, and containing no object class.

This list is definitely for anything placed in the object class line. Would you support a separate table for non-object classes caused by memes/infohazards? I'm not willing to separate Archon and Pending, though. While Pending isn't a true object class in-universe, it's what appears in the articles and it isn't the result of any anomalous manipulation.

item.title: Re: A Less-than-brief Response
item.content:encoded:
+ Rebuttal
- Hide rebuttal

My response to that continues to be that niche object classes aren't interesting content. They're pointless gimmicks that require extra exposition to explain why the object doesn't fit into the S/E/K/T/E/N format, made all the worse by the fact that every object given a 'standard esoteric class' (which is oxymoronic all by itself) could just as easily be given a S/E/K/T/E/N class. Their contribution to site lore is negligible and the avenues they open up for new storytelling possibilities are limited to being able to put them as an object class.

Thaumiel worked because it occupied and defined a unique niche and space in both the object class and Foundation ideology to warrant its existence. Thaumiel is completely unlike Safe, Euclid, and Keter by virtue of the fact that it is not merely contained but actively exploited and relied upon by the Foundation. Moreover, its existence codified the idea that the Foundation was actively utilizing anomalies and even openly acknowledging the hypocrisy of using anomalies to contain anomalies in the name of pragmatism. It worked because it expanded the site lore in a meaningful way.

Archon can be defined in one of two ways: either it's contained by not containing it, in which case it's Safe; or it cannot effectively be contained without causing even more trouble, in which case it's Keter because the Foundation's whole job is to contain things. Th only lore Archon creates is its own pointless existence.

Hiemal is even worse; its author is quick to point out that Roget's Proposal, the original Thaumiel, should in fact be Hiemal — even though the mere statement that the original Thaumiel would work as a Hiemal only confirms Hiemal's sheer pointlessness in the face of Thaumiel's existence.

Apollyon worked thrice — once for shock factor and twice for poignancy — before its own saturation into the site lore ruined its original purpose and caused its creator to abandon it.

Maksur, Ticonderoga, Eparch, Godel, and all the rest are pointless gimmicks that do nothing but hook the reader by virtue of being unconventional, when that unconventionality is completely contrary to the point of having object classes.

TL;DR Niche object classes aren't interesting content. They're pointless gimmicks that don't make sense in-universe and thus require extra exposition to explain why the object doesn't fit into the S/E/K/T/E/N format. This is made all the worse because every object given a 'standard esoteric class' (which is oxymoronic all by itself) could just as easily be given a S/E/K/T/E/N class. Thaumiel was never a pointless gimmick because unlike every other niche object class, it did not fit into the then-standard SEKEN mold and completely changed the Foundation's relationship with anomalies, both pragmatically and ideologically, thus opening up entirely new avenues of storytelling in the format.

item.title: A Less-than-brief Response
item.content:encoded:
+ show block
– hide block

That may be all well and good, but even classes like Thaumiel once held the title of "esoteric". Thaumiel received its own tag after appearing in only two articles.1 Different standards for a smaller site with a different tagging administration, to be sure, but this is no insignificant fact.

With a change in standards, it's harder to create and write for a non-standard class. But that difficulty shouldn't disincentivize writers — Thaumiel was once in the exact same position, and now look at the way we accept it as a narrative conceit. Object Classes are just as plastic as every other aspect of article format. Writers2 like Scantron/CWW have proven just how easily things may bend, given a good enough reason.

There are classes that prevail above others; in the same way, there are esoteric classes that will pass the threshold of "canon" and become standard, like Thaumiel before them. For instance, look at Archon. In the span of one year, writers have written nine separate articles about it.

You could make the case that most esoteric classes are "pointless gimmicks", and I won't deny you that, but some have a decent chance at becoming the next big thing. The higher standards required to make them "a thing" will never dissuade writers from coming up with novel ideas. In fact, since it takes more work to solidify these concepts nowadays, they only feel even more legitimate. And so I would argue that your pushback against esoteric classes is only the driving force to make them stronger and more robust.

TL;DR: We shouldn't disparage the esoteric classes just because they aren't well-known or don't seem "useful" enough. We should instead accept that creators will work very hard to produce interesting content, for which there is always a spot on this website. Thaumiel — an object class you yourself have used, even though it was once a pointless gimmick with no articles to its name — is a strong example.

Footnotes
1. By some measures, receiving a tag is the lower threshold of "canon" on the site.
2. Dare I say trailblazers?

In universe, they make no sense because their nicheness is the exact opposite of what the object class is supposed to achieve — a standardized at-a-glance assessment of the difficulty of containing an object. Out of universe, they're pointless gimmicks used to class an object that inevitably fits perfectly well within the existing Safe-Euclid-Keter-Thaumiel-Explained-Neutralized framework.
